sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text:
Efficient CO2 electrochemical reduction reaction (CO2RR) relies not only on the development of selective/active catalysts but also on advanced electrode configuration to solve the critical issue of poor CO2 mass transport and derived sluggish cathodic reaction kinetics. In this work, to achieve a favorable reaction rate and product selectivity, we designed and synthesized an asymmetric porous Cu hollow fiber gas diffusion electrode (HFGDE) with controlled Sn surface electrodeposition. The HFGDE derived from the optimal Sn electrodeposition condition exhibited a formate faradaic efficiency (FE) of 78% and a current density of 88 mA/cm2 at -1.2 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode, which are more than two times higher than those from the pristine Cu HFGDE. The achieved performance outperformed most of other Sn-based GDEs, indicating the creation of sufficient contact among CO2, electrolyte and electrode catalyst through the design of hollow fiber pore structure and catalytic active sites. The enhancement of formate production selectivity and the suppression of hydrogen by-product was attributed to the optimized ratio of SnOx species on the electrode surface. The best performance was seen for the HFGDE with the highest Sn2+/Sn4+ (120s deposition), likely due to the modulating effect of Cu substrate via electron donation with Sn species. The selectivity control strategy developed in the asymmetric HFGDE provides an efficient and facile method to stimulate selective electrochemical reactions in which gas-phase reactant with low solubility is involved. KEYWORDS: CO2 electrochemical reduction, hollow fiber gas diffusion electrode, composite electrocatalyst, formate formation, Sn electrocatalyst

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2), as the most abundant carbon source, to other carbon-based fuels is a sustainable solution towards achieving a carbon-neutral energy cycle 1-2. The electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) is a promising process because it can be coupled with renewable energies and operated at ambient conditions 3. CO2RR produces diverse valuable compounds, such as formate/formic acid, CO, CH4, and C2H4 which can be further reduced or utilized as a feedstock for other reactions 4. In particular, formate is a useful hydrogen carrier for fuel cell applications with high energy density. However, the efficiency of CO2RR and selectivity of the products must be improved to make CO2RR a viable approach for CO2 conversion. Therefore, the development of efficient catalysts with both high selectivity and high catalytic rate is crucial. Various types of metal-based electrocatalysts have been studied for this process and several comprehensive reviews have been published 5. In brief, metal catalysts can be divided into three groups: 1) Catalysts with high selectivity towards CO, for example, Au and Ag 6, 2) Catalysts with preference to produce formate, such as Sn, Pb, Bi and In 7-9, and 3) Cu, with the unique ability to produce various hydrocarbons at different potentials 10. Sn-based catalysts are an attractive choice for CO2RR to formate because they are highly selective, non-toxic, and have a relatively high overpotential for hydrogen evolution reaction 11-12. The latter is an unwanted side-product and lowers the product efficiency of CO2RR. Sn also increases the selectivity of Cu for formate or CO formation through improved structure and composition in creating an alloy catalyst (Bronze) 13-17.

4 While the catalyst is important for increased selectivity and production rate, the electrode configuration also plays a vital role 18-20. Metal foils or nanocatalysts deposited on a glassy carbon or carbon paper are examples of planar electrode configuration. Here, electrodes are simply immersed in the electrolyte, resulting in a poor mass transport of CO2 towards the electrode with limited feasibility for real applications. Over recent years, gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs) have been successfully employed in applications such as fuel cells 21-22, bioelectrochemical systems 23, and various gas-fed electroreduction processes (O2, CO, CO2 reduction) 8, 24. With GDEs, CO2 is fed to the reactor through the GDE and it contacts the catalyst and electrolyte on the surface of the GDE. This is in contrast to the conventional reactor, where CO2 is sparged to the electrolyte to saturate it 25. Because they exhibit low ohmic loss and high energy efficiency, membrane assembly electrodes and GDEs may improve the feasibility of CO2RR at large scale with commerciallyrelevant current densities (>200 mA cm-2) 25-26. In tackling CO2 mass transport limitation, Han et al. showed that the current density of CO reduction to C2H4 increases from 0.9 to 51 mA cm-2 if CO is fed to the reactor through a GDE instead of purging CO in the electrolyte 27. This is due to a significant increase in the catalytic surface area and formation of three-phase boundaries (catalyst, gas and electrolyte), where the reduction takes place. Planar GDEs have been widely used for CO2RR to various products 28-30. Improvement in partial current density (PCD) was usually observed because of an increase in surface contact area, and better diffusion of reactants and products as compared with planar electrode shape. For example, for formate formation with indium (In), a comparison between In foil and indium-coated gas diffusion electrodes revealed almost 7 times higher partial current densities when GDE was used 29. Although planar GDEs have improved the performance of CO2RR cells, they have some complexities as a separate chamber is usually required for gas transportation. In addition, mass

5 production is limited by economic and technical issues as planar GDEs consist of several layers, e.g. gas diffusion layer, catalyst layer, microporous layer (MPL) 18, 22. Some of these problems can be solved by using hollow fiber gas diffusion electrodes (HFGDEs), a recently considered electrode configuration. HFGDEs provide abundant surface areas to form the three-phase boundary for gas-liquid interface reactions, and owing to the small diameter and tubular shape, the surface area can be easily increased by using more fibers (a bundle of electrodes) without increasing the cell size 31. This, and the ease of inorganic hollow fiber fabrication via the mature and well-studied dry-wet spinning process 32, gives further reactor design flexibility. Cu-based HFGDE was used for CO2RR by Kas et al., who observed that CO formation on copper HFGDE was at least one order of magnitude larger than that using state-of-the-art nanocrystalline copper electrodes 33. This improved performance was due to the properties of oxide-derived Cu with high selectivity towards CO and less for hydrogen evolution. Later, Cu-based HFGDEs were coated with Ni and Au to adjust the binding energy of the CO* intermediate and to decrease the reaction overpotential 34. However, the FE (faradaic efficiency) of CO and partial current density were not improved noticeably, probably because Ni is known to be inert towards CO2RR 35. Bell et al. increased the current density of Cu HFGDE over ten fold by simply treating the particles to make them porous before fabrication. However, FE data were not reported, and the selectivity of that particular HFGDE is unknown 36. Therefore, tuning the product selectivity of the inherently nonselective Cu-based HFGDEs should be addressed via proper catalyst loading approaches, especially for formate formation, as Cu shows poor selectivity towards formate. In this study, we design and synthesize asymmetric HFGDEs for efficient CO2RR to formate, aiming to solve the CO2 solubility issue, and regulate the product selectivity by controllable surface Sn catalyst deposition. Herein, Sn was potentiostatically electrodeposited on Cu HFGDE and a strong correlation was found between the electrodeposition time and surface chemistry of the HFGDEs. The Cu and CuSn HFGDEs were comprehensively analyzed to explore the optimum deposition time and CO2RR performance with different Sn valence states and HFGDE morphology. CuSn HFGDE prepared with optimal deposition showed significantly improved FE for formate (78% at -1.2 V vs. RHE) with 68 mA/cm2 formate partial current density. This study contributes guidance on the design of an asymmetric HFGDE with efficient reaction rate and product selectivity for CO2RR at ambient conditions.

sections.heading: 2.1. HFGDE Fabrication
sections.text:
The HFGDEs were prepared via a dry-wet spinning process 37. Cu powder (99% purity, 5-10 µm, Sandvik, UK) was used as the inorganic precursor for HFGDE fabrication. Cu was first added to N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP, Sigma) as the solvent for phase inversion. After mixing and putting in an ultrasonication bath for 1 h, Polyethersulfone (PES Ultrason E 6020 P, BASF, Germany) as the polymer binder was added to the Cu+NMP solution in a few steps to make sure that the polymer dissolved completely. The final composition of the solution was 65wt%, 8.75wt% and 26.25wt% for Cu powder, polymer and NMP, respectively. The solution was stirred (magnetic) at 60 °C for 6 h following by stirring overnight to ensure the solution was homogenous. The precursor was vacuumed for 1 h to remove bubbles before spinning through a stainless-steel vessel at room temperature. Subsequently, the precursor was pumped through a spinneret rig with

The hollow fibers were kept in the non-solvent bath overnight to finish phase inversion and remove NMP from the hollow fiber structure. After that, the fibers were dried at room temperature. The green hollow fibers were calcinated in the air atmosphere at 650 °C for 2 h (5 °C/min heating and cooling rate) in a tubular furnace to remove the polymer, and induce particle sintering and development of grain boundaries. Subsequently, the fibers were reduced back to Cu by hydrogenation at 500 °C for 1 h (5 °C/min heating and cooling rate) in the H2/Ar atmosphere (H2:20%, Ar:80%). The HFGDEs were kept under the N2 atmosphere before any further tests.

sections.heading: 2.2. Sn Electrodeposition on Cu HFGDE
sections.text:
Sn was loaded on the Cu HFGDE via the well-known facile electrodeposition process 38-39. The electrodeposition electrolyte was prepared in a cylinder shape vessel from the aqueous solution of 0.1M SnCl2.2H2O (Sigma) and 0.4M K4P2O7 (Sigma), as pyrophosphate-based electrolytes result in a stable coating due to improved metal complexes stability and reduced metallic ion activity 40. A tin film (Sn foil 0.1 mm thickness, 99.9%, Nilaco Corporation, Japan) was bent into a cylindrical shape and used as the sacrifice positive electrode, while Cu HFGDE was placed as the working electrode (Schematically shown in Figure S1a). The Sn sheet was pre-treated with 2 M HNO3 for 2 min to remove impurities, rinsed with Milli-Q water and dried with N2 gas. The electrodeposition was done in a three-electrode configuration, where Sn foil, Ag/AgCl and Cu HFGDE were used as the counter, reference and working electrode, respectively. The potential of the working electrode was set to -1 V vs. Ag/AgCl and electrodeposition was carried out at durations from 15s to 300s; the samples were named CuSn15, CuSn30, CuSn60, CuSn120, and CuSn300 based on

Sn was electrodeposited on the outer surface of the Cu HFGDE by electrodeposition at -1 V vs.
Ag/AgCl over 15s to 300s. The morphology, surface composition, CO2 transport, and eventually CO2RR performance of the HFGDEs, can be affected by the electrodeposition duration, as the surface of HFGDEs change from partially covered up to 120s deposition, to fully covered for 300s
and above. Figure 1a schematically shows the electrodeposition of Sn on Cu HFGDE surface and
how CO2 diffuses through the porous structure of the walls, and then reduces to formate on the HFGDE surface. The porous structure of HFGDE facilitates transport of CO2 to the catalyst/electrolyte interface, while the controllable active sites of catalyst on the hollow fiber
surface contribute to the selective reaction. As can be seen from Figure 1b, HFGDEs have a
consistent morphology with a uniform wall thickness of 150-160 µm. The hollow fibers are stable
for handling and can be slightly and gently bent (Figure S2) which makes them practical for real
applications where fragile materials cannot be employed. After Sn electrodeposition, the Cu
HFGDE color gradually turns gray, indicating the formation of a Sn layer on the surface (Figure
1c). In addition, EDX spectra showed no carbon peak, confirming the complete removal of the
polymer binder during calcination (Figure S3). SEM images of the cross-section and the surface
of the Cu and CuSn HFGDEs prepared at different electrodeposition durations, and the
corresponding EDX mapping images are shown in Figure 2. Moreover, high magnification SEM
of the HFGDE surface shows considerable roughness consisting of nanostructures (Figure S4a).
These nanostructures will provide a higher density of low-coordinated sites such as edges and
corners that can bind more strongly with adatoms than flat surfaces, and also possess a high electric
field as a result of their high curvature 42. Therefore, this can contribute to a higher active surface
area and improved current density, and it also facilitates the formation of a stable Sn layer on the
Cu HFGDE.

With electrodeposition, a layer of Sn is deposited on the surface of the Cu HFGDE. As the
electrodeposition time increases, Sn nuclei have more time to grow, therefore the Sn layer becomes
thicker (Figure 2). For 15s electrodeposition, particles smaller than 100 nm are formed (Figure
S4b), and their size increases to around 1 µm for 30s electrodeposition (Figure 2a1). The Sn layer
becomes more continuous with increased deposition time, as the particles start to connect and
partially cover the surface. After 300s, the Sn layer completely covers the electrode as can be seen
in Figures 2a4, 2b4 and 2c4. The high magnification SEM image of CuSn300 also shows the
complete covering of Cu substrate by tight Sn crystals on the surface (Figure S4c). For

were observed on the electrode surface as nuclei continue to grow (Figure S5). The surface of
HFGDEs is rough; Cu particles sized of 5-10 um are sintered and this results in a varying surface

seen with SEM and EDS mapping (Figures 2c1-c4) that the Sn layer becomes denser and more

Deposition time also affects gas permeance through the HFGDEs by possibly blocking the pores,
thereby it can affect CO2 mass transport. For all the HFGDEs in this study, a pressure gradient of 0.6-0.9 bar across the HFGDE was enough to radially pass the gas through, achieving 20 ml/min
gas flow. This is almost half the pressure applied to reach the same flow in another study of a Cu
HFGDE 33. This low gas resistance is an advantage of the HFGDEs developed in the current study
as GDEs are meant to have a gas resistance as low as possible. This feature can be related to using
PES as the binding polymer, because PES exhibits a porous structure after the phase inversion
process 43. Although, the electrodeposition was done while the HFGDEs were purged with Ar (20
ml/min) to keep the pores open, a 60% decrease in the permeance and porosity was observed for
CuSn300 as compared with Cu HFGDE, due to possible pore blockage, more pressure drop
because of increased resistance, and a thicker Sn layer (Figure 2d). However, CuSn120 showed
over 90% gas permeance and porosity compared to Cu HFGDE, with open pores as seen in Figure
2a3, so it can be said that the porous structure of the Cu HFGDE is maintained for electrodeposition
up to 120s. EDX spectra of CuSn120 also showed no visible Sn peak on the cross-section of the
HFGDE, which confirms that deep penetration of Sn and sacrificing of the electrode porosity
during electrodeposition was unlikely (see Figure S3). Moreover, the Mercury intrusion analysis

As shown in the XRD patterns of Cu and CuSn HFGDEs (Figure 3a), clear diffraction peaks
([111], [200], [220]) are visible for Cu in all the electrodes, as X-rays diffuse through the Sn layer
to the Cu substrate 34. Peaks attributed to Sn metal were observed for CuSn HFGDEs and became
stronger as the deposition time increased and more Sn was deposited on the electrode surface.
Using the commercial Sn nanopowder as a reference, it can be seen that Sn facets of [200], [101],
[220], and [211] are formed on the electrode surface after electrodeposition 38.
To deeply study the HFGDEs surface, high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) was used to analyze the
surface composition, and to confirm the presence of crystalline structures. The samples were tested
for HRTEM after a pre-reduction period of 30 min (before CO2RR) and also after the main electrolysis tests. A large number of lattice stripes attributed to Sn and SnOx were observed, as can be seen in Figure 3b, Figure S7 (Inverse Fast Fourier Transition (IFFT) images are included for
clarification). In HRTEM images, the lattice spaces of 0.28 nm and 0.206 nm were related to Sn
(101) and Sn (220), respectively, consistent with the XRD peaks observed for the CuSn electrodes
(Figure 3a). A large number of other lattice spaces were also related to SnO and SnO2 crystals, rather than metal Sn. For example, the lattice space of 0.485 nm is larger than any Sn lattice space,
belonging instead to SnO (001) (Figure S7), and the lattice space of 0.236 nm which is attributed
to SnO2 (200) 44-45. This abundance of oxide species existing on the electrode surface can affect the CO2RR significantly. These oxides were present after electrolysis, and lattice spaces attributed to SnOx were detected for the electrodes after CO2RR (see Figure S8).
XRD results confirmed that the main component of Cu HFGDE is Cu0 metals, and for CuSn
electrodes, Sn0 is the main component formed on Cu substrate. However, surface composition and
valence state of the electrodes cannot be precisely analyzed by XRD. Therefore, XPS analysis was

HFGDE surface before CO2RR (after 30 min pre-reduction) and after CO2RR. XPS surveys of Cu and CuSn HFGDEs can be seen in Figure 3c. The characteristic Cu 2p peak (narrow peak at around
932.5 eV) in Figures 3c, 3e is attributed to metal Cu 46. There are possibly minor Cu oxide species
on the electrode surface as seen in the Cu LMM XPS survey (Figure S9a) or the weak satellite
peaks on Cu 2p spectra of Cu HFGDE (Figure 3e). This phenomenon can be attributed to the
natural oxide layer after HFGDE exposure to air or during XPS high-pressure vacuum, as observed
in a similar study 33. The characteristic Sn 3d peak appears after electrodeposition and it becomes
stronger as electrodeposition time increases (CuSn15 shows weak Sn3d peaks, Figure 3d). Cu
characteristic peaks (Cu 2p and Cu LMM) become weaker with electrodeposition time, and at over
120s Sn electrodeposition (CuSn300 is shown here as the representative), no Cu peaks can be
detected in the XPS survey, due to the formation of a thick and continuous Sn layer as seen in
Figure 2a4.
For all the CuSn electrodes, the characteristic Sn 3d peaks (Sn 3d5/2 and Sn 3d3/2), can be deconvoluted to three peak groups which are attributed to Sn4+, Sn2+, and Sn0 (deconvoluted peaks
can be seen in Figure 3d and Figure S9d). Sn 3d5/2 shows a peak around 486.8 eV which can be assigned to Sn4+ species, and it indicates the presence of SnO2 layer on the surface, as it was also observed in HRTEM images. Two other weaker peaks at around 485.6 eV and 484.7 eV are
assigned to Sn2+ and Sn0, respectively, and it confirms the presence of SnO and Sn metal on the
surface of the electrode. The trend of Sn 3d peaks deconvolution is consistent with other related
studies and the tendency in the peaks was similar with the ones observed in the literature 47-50.
However, XRD analysis did not show any visible SnOx peaks, indicating that the oxide states are a minor phase on the electrode surface 13, 47, 51. Cu/Sn atomic ratio derived from XPS spectra

Interestingly, the duration of Sn deposition had a remarkable effect on the concentration of Sn
species on the electrode surface, as seen in Figure 3f. The Sn2+/Sn4+ ratio increased with Sn
deposition time up to 120s and then it decreased sharply for longer deposition times. Therefore,
for very short (15s) and excessive (300s) deposition duration, Sn4+ is the dominant Sn species on
the HFGDE surface. To minimize the potential oxidation at the surface due to exposure to the air,
CuSn samples after 30 min pre-reduction treatment were quickly cleaned, kept in N2-filled vials, and used for XPS measurement. The 30-min treatment of samples prior to XPS was following the
order: CuSn15, CuSn30, CuSn60, CuSn120, and CuSn300, therefore samples with shorter Sn
treatment, had longer time for potential exposure to air. However, total SnOx content did not change significantly in this order, and for example, samples CuSn30, CuSn60 and CuSn120
showed almost identical Sn0 content, therefore the same SnOx content (Sn2++Sn4+), but different Sn2+/Sn4+ ratio (Figure 3f). Thereby, we could rule out the effect of the testing sequence and sample
handling, and attribute changes in Sn2+/Sn4+ to Sn deposition time. SnOx peaks were observed after electrolysis as well, which confirms the persistence of tin oxide species during CO2RR, as observed in HRTEM images after electrolysis (Figure S8). This is consistent with the recent study
on Sn electrodes for CO2RR 47. It can be concluded that under the reduction potentials utilized in this study Cu and Sn are predominantly in their zero-valent valence state, in accordance with the
standard redox potential expectations. However, Sn oxide species with different Sn2+/Sn4+ ratios
are abundant on the surface of the CuSn HFGDEs. This can affect the CO2RR performance,

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrochemical Reduction of CO2
sections.text:
The performance of Cu and CuSn HFGDEs for CO2RR was analyzed through various electrochemical tests, with the results shown in Figure 4. The linear scanning voltammograms of
all HFGDEs (Figure S10) follow a similar trend with low current densities at less negative
potentials, increasing sharply at higher overpotentials when hydrogen evolution reaction and
CO2RR start to compete. It was observed that up to 120s, Sn electrodeposition results in overall higher current density as compared with Cu HFGDE, attributed to the higher electrochemical
active surface area. Electrochemical active surface area is estimated by the electric double-layer
capacitance (Cdl) in Figure 4b, and Cdl increases with Sn electrodeposition time. The highresolution surface SEM images of CuSn HFGDEs (Figure S4a, b and Figure S6) revealed the
formation of a rough surface, consisting of nanostructures around 50 nm in size. This can improve
the surface area for electrolysis and contribute to high current density. For HFGDEs with Sn
deposition over 120s, Cdl decreased along with a reduction in the current density, probably due to the formation of a fairly smooth Sn layer on the electrode surface (Cdl measurement from CV cycles for CuSn120 HFGDE is shown in Figure S11 as an example). A significantly higher current
density was seen when CO2 was passed through the Cu and CuSn120 HFGDEs, as compared with Ar (Figure 4a). The current measured with Ar is related to hydrogen evolution reaction from the
water splitting half-reaction on the cathode, and when CO2 is fed through to the HFGDE, CO2 reduction occurs and competes with the hydrogen evolution reaction. The reduction current density
under Ar was very similar for both Cu and CuSn120 HFGDEs (green and black dash-lines in
Figure 4a), while under CO2 (green and black lines in Figure 4a), CuSn120 HFGDE showed a higher current density than Cu HFGDE. This increase in the current density with CO2 comes from the high electrocatalytic activity of HFGDEs towards CO2RR. Moreover, when CO2 is fed to the

fiber shape as the electrode and for gas delivery in terms of efficient electron, gas and ion transport
at the triple-phase boundaries 27.
The chronoamperometry experiments were applied to examine the short-time stability of HFGDEs
over a 1 h constant potential test between -0.4 V to -1.4 V vs. RHE with 0.2 V intervals. Liquid
and gas samples were collected to measure FE of varied products. Sampling was done at least 30
min after changing the potential to make sure of the steady-state condition. During
chronoamperometry, current density remained stable during 1 h electrolysis with no considerable
changes for all the samples (as an example, chronoamperometry profiles of CuSn120 HFGDE at
different potentials are shown in Figure S12a). The total FE was 90-100% for overall H2, CO and formate formation, indicating that the charge-transfer mostly contributed to the formation of these
products. The FE of formate, H2, and CO are shown in Figure S12b, c, and d, respectively. Due to the nature of Cu HDGDE fabrication, which involves oxidation and reduction of Cu during the
thermal process, these oxide-derived Cu electrodes have been shown to have relatively lower FE
for hydrogen evolution reaction, along with relatively higher FE for formate and CO as compared
with polycrystalline Cu 53. It is known that FE, current density and onset of different products on
Cu-based electrocatalysts strongly depend on the electrode preparation method 54-55. Here, Cu and
CuSn15 HFGDEs showed similar CO2RR performance as Cu was still dominant on the electrode surface (Cu/Sn=5.5 for CuSn15, Figure 3d). They were both relatively selective towards CO
formation (53-64% FE, Figure S12d) at more positive potentials (-0.4 to -0.8 V vs. RHE), which
is consistent with similar studies on Cu HFGDE 33-34. The minor formation of CH4 and C2H4, with total FE of 4-11% at more negative potentials (-1 to -1.4 V vs. RHE), was observed for CuSn15,

CuSn30 and CuSn60 HFGDEs, confirming the participation of Cu substrate in CO2RR at short Sn deposition times.
The HFGDEs showed higher FE for formate formation at potentials -1 to -1.2 V vs. RHE, as this
is the common potential window to reduce CO2 to formate on Sn-based electrocatalysts 38, 47, 56-57. As Sn electrodeposition time increased, FE of formate increased, since Sn-based species became
dominant on the electrode surface with deposition time (Cu/Sn=0.06 for CuSn120, Figure 3d), and
took part to convert CO2 to formate 12, 45, 58. As seen in Figure 4c, CuSn60 and CuSn120 have a formate FE of 73% and 78% at -1 and -1.2 V vs. RHE, respectively, which is more than 2 times
compared to Cu HFGDE (28% at -1.2 V vs. RHE). The highest formate partial current density
(PCD = current density × FE of formate) is also observed for CuSn120 HFGDE at -1.2 V vs. RHE
with around 68 mA/cm2 (Figure 4d). For the potentials more negative than -1.2 V vs. RHE (-1.4
V vs. RHE was studied here), hydrogen evolution became severe and increased for all the HFGDEs
(Figure S12c) along with a decrease in FE of formate (Figure S12b), as observed in other studies
38, 59, hence, more negative potentials were not studied here.
The selectivity of CO2RR towards formate highly depends on the oxidation state of the Sn species 49, 52, 57. Here, the improvement in the FE of Cu HFGDE for formate formation after Sn
electrodeposition can be explained by looking at the changes of the surface chemistry of the
HFGDEs with the deposition time. Sn electrodes are known to possess a native oxide layer 60-61,
and as it was confirmed in the XPS and HRTEM results, Sn forms a metastable oxide layer on the
surface which persists on the electrode surface under cathodic reactions. The potentials studied
here are more negative than the standard potential of SnO and SnO2 reduction, but SnOx species were observed after electrolysis using XPS (Figure S9d) and HRTEM (Figure S8) of the electrode

from 6.7% before CO2RR to 12.8% after CO2RR for CuSn120, Figure S9d), SnOx were the dominant species on the electrode surface. This is consistent with the results from Chen’s study
that after 12 h electrolysis, native SnOx still exists with minimal reduction to Sn0, and oxide species can reconstitute on the electrode surface during the actual CO2RR process 52. In fact, the simultaneous presence of Sn and SnOx on the electrode surface increases the energy barrier for hydrogen evolution, thereby it can suppress hydrogen production and lead to an increment in FE
of formate formation. In accordance with our results, other studies have lately shown that SnOx has much higher ability to reduce CO2 to formate as compared with metal Sn, and that a mixed oxidation state (Sn/SnOx) has the highest formate yield 57, while Sn catalyst with no oxide layer shows a high H2 evolution activity 52. Wu et al. specifically studied the effect of Sn oxide layer thickness and observed that the native oxide layer (with a thickness of around 3.5 nm) has a better
FE for formate formation than thicker oxide layers 60.

The results from the current study suggest that formate formation on CuSn HFGDEs can be tuned
by optimizing the Sn2+/Sn4+ ratio with the Sn deposition time. The ratio of SnOx species was found to be highly dependent on the electrodeposition time, as seen in Figure 4c, with CuSn120
exhibiting the best performance for formate formation, having the highest Sn2+/Sn4+ ratio. This
demonstrates the importance of a suitable Sn2+/Sn4+ ratio for optimum CO2RR efficiency. Liu’s work revealed that Sn4+ plays an essential role in CO2RR 49, while An et al. reported on the effective role of Sn2+ and claimed that a suitable ratio of Sn0/Sn2+/Sn4+ on the electrode surface is
necessary to obtain the highest FE for formate formation 47. Here, we observed that the best
performance for formate formation is achieved at the maximum Sn2+/Sn4+ ratio. Based on the
formate FE results and changes in Sn2+/Sn4+ ratio with deposition time, it can be said that the
presence of Cu on the HFGDE surface and contact with the electrodeposition solution (for
electrodes with Sn deposition up to 120s) has an important modulating effect on the ratio, resulting
in an improved FE. Cu/Sn atomic ratio for CuSn120 is 0.06 (Figure 3d), which makes Sn-based
species the dominant on the surface, however the existing Cu can still affect CO2RR performance by modulating the Sn species during electrodeposition. Sn valence states and Sn2+/Sn4+ ratio can
be affected by neighboring Cu via electron donations between Sn species and Cu 17, 62. This can be
explained by considering the electronegativity of Cu which falls between that of Sn0 and SnOx species (larger than SnOx species but smaller than Sn0) 63-64. Therefore, it will affect the ratio of Sn species by donating an electron to its neighboring Sn atoms or withdrawing from SnOx species. This is for electrodeposition time up to 120s as Cu is still detected on the surface by XPS (Figure
3e). For excess electrodeposition time, e.g. 300s, the HFGDE surface was fully covered, and Sn2+
content dropped sharply, along with a marked reduction in formate formation and increment in
hydrogen evolution (Figure S12c). CuSn300 electrode showed formate FE of 63-67% between -1

For practical applications, the HFGDE stability is as important as high catalytic activity. Therefore,
CuSn120 HFGDE was chosen for a 4 h short-term stability measurement at -1.2 V vs. RHE, and
the results of formate partial current density and FE of formate, H2 and CO can be seen in Figure 4e. The sampling was done every 30 min and the HFGDE showed good current stability with a
slight decrease in formate conversion to around 73% after 4 h, along with a slight increment in FE
of hydrogen evolution. However, PCD of formate remained close to steady, with a slight rise in
the overall current density during the test. Hori et al. showed that the activity of polycrystalline Cu
diminishes quickly (within an hour), unless high purity electrolytes and electrodes (99.9999%) are
utilized 65. Considering the relatively lower purity of the Cu precursor in this study (99%), which
significantly reduces the price for commercial application, HFGDEs presented a stable
performance. In addition, the reaction took place in a batch mode operation, therefore, there may
have been some changes in the ion concentration, pH or temperature which can affect performance
59, 66. Narayanan et al. observed that the FE of formate formation on In catalyst decreases after a
few hours of operation in an H-cell, assumed to be because of the reduced availability of
bicarbonate and CO2 for reduction at the surface of the electrode due to build-up of diffusion barriers 67. Therefore, the development of flow-type reactors working with HFGDEs may improve
the efficiency and stability of the reaction and products.
The performance of the fabricated HFGDEs here in terms of current density and FE of formate
was compared to other Sn-based GDEs and non-GDEs in the literature (Figure 4f and Table S1).

based catalysts (70-90 %). In particular, non-GDE electrode configuration shows higher FE (up to
95%) but suffers from low current density (lower than 10 mA/cm2). GDEs have been able to
improve current density, however, the current density observed in this study outperforms most
GDEs. This arises from the unique structure and shape of the hollow fiber electrode which
enhances CO2 delivery without sacrificing catalytic active area as a result of using polymeric binders (Table S1). We observed rough surfaces in high-resolution SEM images for both Cu and
CuSn HFGDEs (Figures S4, S6) which contribute to a higher CD as compared with conventional
GDEs (Figure 4f). The performance can be further improved by designing a flow-cell reactor or
providing more active Sn sites via surface engineering. For example, sulfur is a promising
modulator for both Sn and In sites to improve both current density and FE of formate formation 68,
69. Similar approaches can be considered for tuning the active sites on the Cu substrate, taking
advantage of attributes of the hollow fiber electrode.
The results of strategic design of HFGDEs for CO2RR to formate in this study showed that HFGDEs potentially circumvent the issues of conventional planar GDEs, and solve the critical
issue of low reaction rate in an aqueous CO2RR. Using HFGDEs can reduce the cell complexity by supplying CO2 through the fiber lumen, and CO2 diffusing to the active sites through the porous wall. Therefore, no gas chamber is required in the cell for gas transportation, and the electrode
surface area can be increased with a bundle of fibers, without increasing reactor size. Moreover,
HFGDEs can be fabricated in small radial dimensions to maximize the ratio of surface area to
volume and specific surface area of the cathode, thus allowing more efficient CO2 gas diffusion, enhanced charge transfer, and higher cathode catalysts packing density than planar GDEs.

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSION
sections.text:
Controlled electrodeposition of Sn catalyst on the porous Cu hollow fiber to fabricate composite
HFGDEs offers a facile and effective route to achieve improved current density with controllable
reaction selectivity for electrochemical CO2 reduction. The electrodeposition duration impacts on HFGDE pore geometry, permeability, surface Sn morphology and Sn valance state, leading to
substantial changes in formate formation selectivity. The HFGDEs prepared with 60 s and 120 s
Sn electrodeposition at -1 V vs. Ag/AgCl displayed significantly improved FE for formate, likely
owing to optimization of the Sn2+/Sn4+ ratio on HFGDE surface. However, excess Sn deposition
resulted in complete coverage of the Cu hollow fiber substrate and significant hydrogen evolution
reaction. As different Sn/SnOx species are essential for optimal performance of CO2RR to formate formation, it was concluded that the presence of Cu is necessary to modulate the suitable Sn2+/Sn4+
ratio on the surface, possibly via electron donation between Cu and Sn species, considering their
electronegativity. In terms of formate FE and current density, HFGDEs outperformed most of the
referenced Sn-based GDEs, owing to their unique tubular porous structure with abundant sites for
three-phase reaction and CO2 transportation. For a broader interest, this work provides a technical method to design efficient composite electrodes to overcome the critical issues of mass transfer
and reaction sites in aqueous electrochemical reactions.
